screens.title: Introduction to BGP
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter you will develop a clear, practical understanding of BGP — the protocol that enables enterprises to connect to the wider internet and to express routing policy across administrative boundaries. We will define what an Autonomous System is, explain why BGP is used between ASes while IGPs operate within them, and show how BGP’s path vector behavior prevents loops and enables policy decisions. You'll see a realistic multi‑homed enterprise scenario where BGP lets an organization choose which ISP to use for outgoing traffic and how to remain resilient when a link fails. We will also cover common beginner mistakes, such as confusing BGP with IGPs or misusing AS numbers, and give you a short hands‑on identification activity to reinforce learning. By the end of this chapter you'll understand when to run eBGP or iBGP, what information is shared in route advertisements, and why AS_PATH matters. Think about your own network: where would you place your BGP peers and which policies would you need to express? That question will guide our practical examples.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will build four distinct competencies that matter for any enterprise network engineer. First, you will explain why BGP is necessary for inter‑domain routing: you should be able to describe how Autonomous Systems connect and why policy, not just shortest path, drives decisions. Second, you will differentiate BGP from IGPs like OSPF — articulating that IGPs optimize intra‑AS reachability and fast convergence while BGP handles inter‑AS policy and reachability. Third, you will identify and define core BGP concepts: Autonomous System numbers, eBGP, iBGP, BGP speakers, prefixes, and the AS_PATH attribute, and explain how each contributes to loop prevention and policy. Fourth, you will recognize typical enterprise scenarios such as multi‑homing and ISP failover where BGP is indispensable. Each objective includes a practical example and a competency milestone so you can verify understanding. As you work through the lesson, keep a checklist of these competencies and test them against the hands‑on scenario at the end of the chapter.

screens.title: Autonomous Systems (AS)
screens.narratorSegment: An Autonomous System, or AS, is a group of IP networks and routers operated under a single administrative domain that presents a unified routing policy to the rest of the internet. AS numbers uniquely identify that domain so BGP speakers can advertise where prefixes originate and which administrative path those advertisements took. For example, an enterprise assigned AS 65000 advertises its public prefixes to its ISP peers using that AS number. This AS identity isn't decorative: when route advertisements include AS numbers, receivers can read the AS_PATH attribute to see the sequence of ASes a route traversed. That sequence enables two vital functions. First, it prevents routing loops: if you see your own AS number in the path, you discard the route. Second, it enables policy decisions: an operator can prefer or reject routes based on which ASes are present in the path or the path's length. A common misconception is to treat AS numbers like arbitrary labels; instead, they are operationally significant and must be unique in inter‑AS contexts. When planning a multi‑homed setup, use distinct, correctly assigned AS numbers and ensure your route advertisements present the correct origin AS. Consider the practical example of AS 65000 advertising 198.51.100.0/24 to ISPs; the AS number identifies the origin and informs downstream policy and loop prevention.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Autonomous Systems (AS)
Definition

Autonomous System (AS)

A unique administrative domain identified by an AS number. AS numbers appear in BGP advertisements and the AS_PATH attribute.

Concrete example
Enterprise AS 65000 advertises 198.51.100.0/24. That AS number marks the origin in AS_PATH.
Common misconception
AS numbers are not cosmetic tags — they control loop prevention and are used in policy decisions.
Key Takeaway

Use a correct, unique AS number. The AS number matters operationally for AS_PATH-based loop prevention and policy.

Annotated cards
AS number types
Publicly assigned (RIR) or private ranges for lab use
Operational role
Identifies origin and path for advertisements, enabling loop checks and policy decisions.
Example label
AS 65000 — enterprise; AS 100 — ISP

screens.title: BGP vs IGPs
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between BGP and Interior Gateway Protocols like OSPF or IS‑IS is foundational. IGPs run inside an AS to provide fast convergence and low-latency path selection based on metrics such as cost or bandwidth. They aim for quick reaction to topology changes so internal hosts remain reachable. BGP, in contrast, operates between ASes and focuses on policy: it lets operators express preferences about which external networks to use for given destinations. For example, an enterprise choosing between two ISPs will use BGP attributes and local policy to prefer one ISP for business-critical traffic and the other for bulk transfers. A common pitfall is to expect BGP to converge as quickly as an IGP; it does not prioritize shortest metric-based paths and may be intentionally constrained by policy choices. Another misconception is to run BGP where an IGP suffices; BGP introduces policy complexity and is necessary only for inter‑AS routing or for expressing advanced inbound/outbound policy in multi‑homed environments. In practice, these protocols complement each other: use an IGP for intra‑AS reachability and fast reroute, and BGP to advertise prefixes and shape traffic between ASes. Ask yourself: where is policy more important than pure path cost in your network?

keyIdea.text: IGPs optimize intra‑AS reachability and fast convergence; BGP enables inter‑AS policy and controlled advertisement of prefixes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › BGP vs IGPs
Comparison

IGP vs BGP — intent and behavior

IGP (e.g., OSPF)
Focus on fast convergence, shortest metric paths, and intra‑AS reachability.
BGP
Focus on inter‑AS policy, prefix advertisement, and AS_PATH-based decisions.
Practical example
Your internal routers run OSPF to keep internal routes updated quickly. Your edge routers run BGP with two ISPs to manage cost and failover. You use OSPF for next‑hop reachability inside the AS and BGP to decide which ISP advertises your prefixes and how incoming traffic is influenced.
Misconception check
Don’t expect BGP to replace an IGP’s role of fast internal convergence.

screens.title: eBGP and iBGP
screens.narratorSegment: BGP peerings fall into two categories: eBGP, which connects routers in different Autonomous Systems, and iBGP, which connects routers within the same AS. eBGP is what an enterprise uses to talk to its ISPs; it exchanges route advertisements between distinct administrative domains and typically sets next‑hop and MED attributes that influence external routing. iBGP distributes externally learned routes inside the AS so that every BGP speaker has a consistent view of what prefixes exist outside the AS. For example, enterprise AS 65000 will use eBGP to learn routes from ISP A and ISP B. Inside AS 65000, internal routers form iBGP sessions so they can forward traffic to the edge routers that learned those external routes. A frequent confusion is to assume that routes learned via iBGP are automatically redistributed by IGPs — iBGP only shares BGP attributes; you must ensure next‑hop reachability via your IGP and respect iBGP rules such as the split‑horizon behavior (iBGP speakers do not re-advertise routes learned from other iBGP peers by default). Remember: eBGP handles inter‑AS exchange, iBGP handles internal distribution of those external routes. Think about the enterprise with two ISPs: without iBGP, internal routers would not reliably learn how to reach external prefixes through the correct edge router.

keyIdea.title: Peer types
keyIdea.text: eBGP connects different ASes for inter‑AS routing; iBGP shares those learned routes inside the same AS so internal routers can forward traffic correctly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › eBGP and iBGP
Process Flow

eBGP ↔ iBGP workflow

Step 1 — eBGP peers learn prefixes
Edge router learns prefix 203.0.113.0/24 from ISP A via eBGP.
Step 2 — iBGP shares route inside AS
Edge router advertises the route to internal BGP peers so core routers know where to send traffic.
Step 3 — IGP ensures next‑hop reachability
An IGP like OSPF is used to make sure the BGP next hop is reachable from internal routers.
Scenario card
AS 65000 connects to ISP A (AS 100) and ISP B (AS 200). eBGP is used to exchange prefixes with AS 100 and AS 200. Inside AS 65000, iBGP sessions distribute those external routes so any internal host can reach the internet through the appropriate edge router.
Common pitfall
Relying on iBGP alone without ensuring IGP next‑hop reachability causes internal traffic blackholes.

screens.title: Path Vector and AS_PATH
screens.narratorSegment: BGP is classified as a path vector protocol because route advertisements carry the sequence of Autonomous Systems a prefix has passed through — the AS_PATH attribute. This explicit path information does two important things. First, it makes loop detection straightforward: if a router sees its own AS in the AS_PATH, it drops the route, preventing traffic from circulating indefinitely. Second, AS_PATH enables operators to make policy decisions based on which ASes are present or on path length. For example, if a route advertises AS_PATH [100 300 400], a router in AS 300 sees that the route passed through AS 100 and then came to 300; if 300 is the receiver and its own AS appears in the path, it will not accept that route due to loop detection. A practical enterprise example: when AS 65000 receives two routes to the same prefix, one with AS_PATH length 2 and another length 4, the operator might prefer the shorter AS_PATH as a simple tiebreaker or write policy that prefers routes avoiding specific ASes. A common misconception is to assume AS_PATH length always implies performance; AS_PATH conveys administrative traversal, not latency. Use AS_PATH for loop prevention and policy, but validate actual performance using telemetry and path testing.

keyIdea.text: AS_PATH is a record of ASes a route traversed; it prevents loops and supports policy decisions, though it does not equal path performance.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Path Vector and AS_PATH
Definition

Path vector and AS_PATH

AS_PATH lists the sequence of AS numbers that a route advertisement traversed. It is used for loop detection and policy decisions.
Concrete example
Route to 203.0.113.0/24 arrives with AS_PATH [100 200]. A router in AS 200 sees the path and avoids re-accepting if AS 200 is in the list.
Policy vs performance
Don't equate shorter AS_PATH with lower latency. AS_PATH is administrative; use measurements to confirm performance before preferring a route solely on AS_PATH length.
Key Takeaway

AS_PATH prevents loops and supports policy decisions but is not a direct measure of path quality.

screens.title: Multi‑homing and failover
screens.narratorSegment: Multi‑homing is when an enterprise connects to two or more ISPs simultaneously. BGP is the protocol that makes multi‑homing practical because it allows the enterprise to advertise prefixes to multiple upstream providers and to control which provider traffic uses for egress and ingress. In a typical setup, AS 65000 peers with ISP A (AS 100) and ISP B (AS 200) via eBGP. The enterprise advertises its public prefixes to both ISPs and learns external routes from both. To control outgoing traffic, the enterprise can set local preference or use AS_PATH prepending to make one path less attractive. For incoming traffic, BGP provides mechanisms to influence which ISP external networks prefer, though complete control is not guaranteed. The resilience benefit is straightforward: if one ISP link fails, BGP withdraws routes learned from that ISP and traffic naturally shifts to the remaining provider. A common novice error is to assume multi‑homing with BGP automatically yields equal load across ISPs; actual traffic distribution depends on global routing decisions and requires deliberate policy to shape. In practice, ensure your internal routers receive external routes via iBGP and that your IGP provides next‑hop reachability so failover occurs smoothly. Consider the enterprise example: test failover by simulating an ISP outage and observe route withdrawal and reconvergence to validate your policy and reachability behavior.

keyIdea.title: Resilience by policy
keyIdea.text: BGP enables multi‑homing by advertising prefixes to multiple ISPs and controlling egress/ingress with attributes like local preference and AS_PATH manipulations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Multi‑homing and failover
Architecture

Enterprise multi‑homing pattern

Enterprise AS advertises prefixes to multiple ISPs and uses BGP attributes to influence which path is chosen for traffic. If one ISP fails, BGP withdraws those routes and the remaining ISP takes over, given correct internal distribution and reachability.
Control egress
Local preference or outbound policy selects which ISP carries outbound flows.
Influence ingress
AS_PATH prepending or selective advertisement can nudge remote ASes to prefer one ISP.
Scenario card
AS 65000 uses eBGP to ISP A and ISP B. It advertises 198.51.100.0/24 to both. If ISP A’s link drops, routes from ISP A are withdrawn and traffic moves to ISP B after BGP reconvergence and IGP reachability checks.
Common mistake
Assuming symmetric traffic distribution without explicit policy or coordination with ISPs.

screens.title: Identify eBGP and iBGP in a diagram
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a simple labeling activity you will encounter in the assessment. Imagine Enterprise A — AS 65001 — and Enterprise B — AS 65002 — both connect to ISP AS 100. Each enterprise has two internal routers. The links between each enterprise and the ISP are eBGP peerings because they cross AS boundaries. Inside each enterprise, the internal routers form iBGP sessions so that routes learned from the ISP are available throughout the AS. To trace a prefix originating in AS 65001 and reaching a host in AS 65002, follow these steps: AS 65001’s border router advertises the prefix to AS 100 via eBGP; AS 100 propagates the route through its own AS and advertises to AS 65002 via eBGP; the border router in AS 65002 receives the prefix and uses iBGP to share it with its internal routers so the destination host can be reached. A frequent learner error is mislabeling internal pairings as eBGP or forgetting that the ISP‑to‑enterprise links are eBGP. As you label diagrams, confirm each peering's AS numbers: if they differ, it's eBGP; if they match, it's iBGP. Try drawing arrows for route advertisement direction to solidify your understanding.

keyIdea.text: Label connections by AS number: different AS numbers indicate eBGP; identical AS numbers inside a domain indicate iBGP. Trace advertisements to verify reachability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Identify eBGP and iBGP
Activity

Label the peerings and trace the path

Given the diagram of Enterprise A (AS 65001), ISP (AS 100), and Enterprise B (AS 65002), mark eBGP on the inter‑AS links and iBGP on internal links. Then draw arrows showing how a prefix from AS 65001 reaches a host in AS 65002 via AS 100.
Check answers
1) Links between different AS numbers are eBGP. 2) Links between routers with the same AS number are iBGP. 3) Route travels via eBGP to the ISP, through the ISP, then via eBGP to the destination AS and is distributed internally via iBGP.
Mini diagram
[Enterprise A] AS 65001
eBGP → [ISP] AS 100 → eBGP → [Enterprise B] AS 65002
Internal routers in each enterprise connect via iBGP to share external routes.
Pro tip
Always verify AS numbers printed on diagrams when labeling peer types.

screens.title: BGP Speaker and Prefixes
screens.narratorSegment: In BGP terminology, a BGP speaker is simply a router running the BGP protocol that sends and receives route advertisements. A prefix is the network block being advertised, such as 192.0.2.0/24. When a BGP speaker advertises a prefix, it sends that prefix along with attributes like AS_PATH, next hop, and potentially MED or communities. The function of the BGP speaker is to originate, propagate, and apply policy to routes. For example, a border router in AS 65000 configured as a BGP speaker advertises its public prefix 198.51.100.0/24 to ISP peers. Those peers receive the prefix and add their own AS number to AS_PATH when they forward the route. A common misconception is to assume every router in the AS must be a BGP speaker; in many deployments a subset of edge and core routers speak BGP while others rely on internal distribution via iBGP and IGP. Another practical point is that prefixes must be announced intentionally: avoid accidentally advertising internal-only networks to the internet. In your design, choose which routers are BGP speakers, plan which prefixes to advertise, and ensure your policies prevent accidental leak of private addressing.

A common misconception is to assume every router in the AS must be a BGP speaker; in many deployments a subset of edge and core routers speak BGP while others rely on internal distribution via iBGP and IGP. Another practical point is that prefixes must be announced intentionally: avoid accidentally advertising internal-only networks to the internet. Definition

BGP speaker & prefix

BGP speaker: a router running BGP. Prefix: a network block announced in BGP, e.g., 198.51.100.0/24.
Concrete example
Border router in AS 65000 advertises 198.51.100.0/24 to ISP peers; those peers add their AS numbers to AS_PATH when relaying the route.
Operational guidance
Decide which routers are BGP speakers and restrict prefixes to those you intend to publish. Avoid leaking internal-only networks to external peers.
Common mistake
Accidentally advertising private addressing to the internet due to misconfigured export policies.

screens.title: Misconfigurations and misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: When learning BGP, several recurring mistakes appear. First, confusing eBGP and iBGP: labeling peerings incorrectly can lead to broken expectations about route propagation. Remember the rule: different AS numbers mean eBGP; identical AS numbers mean iBGP. Second, neglecting IGP next‑hop reachability: BGP may advertise a route, but if your internal network cannot reach the route's next hop, traffic will blackhole. Third, assuming AS_PATH equals performance: AS_PATH records administrative traversal, not latency, so prefer measured metrics for performance-sensitive routing. Fourth, accidentally leaking prefixes: without careful export filters, you might advertise internal or private prefixes to the internet. Finally, not planning for multi‑homing behavior: traffic distribution is influenced by remote AS policies; don’t assume symmetric inbound/outbound flows. Each misconception can be mitigated by disciplined planning: verify AS numbers on diagrams, ensure IGP reachability, use route filtering to prevent leaks, and test failover scenarios to confirm behavior. As a practical check, when you configure a BGP peering in lab or production, validate the advertised AS_PATH and test reachability from multiple internal hosts before trusting the network for critical services. screens.title: Design checklist for introducing BGP
screens.narratorSegment: Before enabling BGP in an enterprise environment, follow a concise checklist to avoid common operational problems. First, assign and verify your AS number; ensure it is appropriate for your environment and does not conflict with your peers. Second, decide which routers will act as BGP speakers and which prefixes you will advertise. Third, plan IGP reachability so BGP next hops are reachable by internal routers. Fourth, create export and import filters to prevent accidental prefix leaks and to control which external routes you accept. Fifth, design iBGP topology to distribute external routes reliably — consider full mesh or route reflectors depending on scale. Sixth, document failover behavior and test simulated outages to validate that route withdrawal and reconvergence behave as expected. A common misconception is that enabling BGP alone provides immediate resilience; the protocol must be paired with correct internal routing and policy controls. Finally, include monitoring and verification steps: confirm AS_PATHs, check advertised prefixes, and validate traffic paths post‑deployment. Use this checklist as a pre‑deployment gating process to reduce surprises when BGP interactions begin with external ASes. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three essential concepts to carry forward. First, Autonomous Systems (AS) are unique administrative domains identified by AS numbers; these numbers matter operationally because they appear in route attributes and enable loop prevention. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will develop a clear, practical understanding of BGP — the protocol that enables enterprises to connect to the wider internet and to express routing policy across administrative boundaries. We will define what an Autonomous System is, explain why BGP is used between ASes while IGPs operate within them, and show how BGP’s path vector behavior prevents loops and enables policy decisions. You'll see a realistic multi‑homed enterprise scenario where BGP lets an organization choose which ISP to use for outgoing traffic and how to remain resilient when a link fails. We will also cover common beginner mistakes, such as confusing BGP with IGPs or misusing AS numbers, and give you a short hands‑on identification activity to reinforce learning. By the end of this chapter you'll understand when to run eBGP or iBGP, what information is shared in route advertisements, and why AS_PATH matters. Think about your own network: where would you place your BGP peers and which policies would you need to express? That question will guide our practical examples.

In this chapter you will build four distinct competencies that matter for any enterprise network engineer. First, you will explain why BGP is necessary for inter‑domain routing: you should be able to describe how Autonomous Systems connect and why policy, not just shortest path, drives decisions. Second, you will differentiate BGP from IGPs like OSPF — articulating that IGPs optimize intra‑AS reachability and fast convergence while BGP handles inter‑AS policy and reachability. Third, you will identify and define core BGP concepts: Autonomous System numbers, eBGP, iBGP, BGP speakers, prefixes, and the AS_PATH attribute, and explain how each contributes to loop prevention and policy. Fourth, you will recognize typical enterprise scenarios such as multi‑homing and ISP failover where BGP is indispensable. Each objective includes a practical example and a competency milestone so you can verify understanding. As you work through the lesson, keep a checklist of these competencies and test them against the hands‑on scenario at the end of the chapter.

Let's unpack how you will demonstrate these objectives in practice. For explaining BGP's purpose, you'll articulate a multi‑homed enterprise example where two ISPs provide different performance or cost attributes and BGP is used to select egress points. For differentiating BGP and IGPs, you'll explain why an IGP's rapid convergence is not sufficient for inter‑AS policy and give a short contrast example. For defining core concepts, you'll list AS numbers, describe prefixes and AS_PATH and demonstrate how AS_PATH prevents loops with a concrete small AS chain. For recognizing scenarios, you'll map the hands‑on diagram at the end: labeling eBGP peerings between enterprises and ISPs, and iBGP peerings inside ASes to distribute externally learned routes. Each objective ties to a simple verification task: a short explanation or a diagram label. Use that checklist while you study: it keeps conceptual learning aligned with practical recognition and prevents common misconceptions such as using iBGP between different ASes or thinking AS numbers are arbitrary tags rather than functional identifiers.

An Autonomous System, or AS, is a group of IP networks and routers operated under a single administrative domain that presents a unified routing policy to the rest of the internet. AS numbers uniquely identify that domain so BGP speakers can advertise where prefixes originate and which administrative path those advertisements took. For example, an enterprise assigned AS 65000 advertises its public prefixes to its ISP peers using that AS number. This AS identity isn't decorative: when route advertisements include AS numbers, receivers can read the AS_PATH attribute to see the sequence of ASes a route traversed. That sequence enables two vital functions. First, it prevents routing loops: if you see your own AS number in the path, you discard the route. Second, it enables policy decisions: an operator can prefer or reject routes based on which ASes are present in the path or the path's length. A common misconception is to treat AS numbers like arbitrary labels; instead, they are operationally significant and must be unique in inter‑AS contexts. When planning a multi‑homed setup, use distinct, correctly assigned AS numbers and ensure your route advertisements present the correct origin AS. Consider the practical example of AS 65000 advertising 198.51.100.0/24 to ISPs; the AS number identifies the origin and informs downstream policy and loop prevention.

Understanding the difference between BGP and Interior Gateway Protocols like OSPF or IS‑IS is foundational. IGPs run inside an AS to provide fast convergence and low-latency path selection based on metrics such as cost or bandwidth. They aim for quick reaction to topology changes so internal hosts remain reachable. BGP, in contrast, operates between ASes and focuses on policy: it lets operators express preferences about which external networks to use for given destinations. For example, an enterprise choosing between two ISPs will use BGP attributes and local policy to prefer one ISP for business-critical traffic and the other for bulk transfers. A common pitfall is to expect BGP to converge as quickly as an IGP; it does not prioritize shortest metric-based paths and may be intentionally constrained by policy choices. Another misconception is to run BGP where an IGP suffices; BGP introduces policy complexity and is necessary only for inter‑AS routing or for expressing advanced inbound/outbound policy in multi‑homed environments. In practice, these protocols complement each other: use an IGP for intra‑AS reachability and fast reroute, and BGP to advertise prefixes and shape traffic between ASes. Ask yourself: where is policy more important than pure path cost in your network?

BGP peerings fall into two categories: eBGP, which connects routers in different Autonomous Systems, and iBGP, which connects routers within the same AS. eBGP is what an enterprise uses to talk to its ISPs; it exchanges route advertisements between distinct administrative domains and typically sets next‑hop and MED attributes that influence external routing. iBGP distributes externally learned routes inside the AS so that every BGP speaker has a consistent view of what prefixes exist outside the AS. For example, enterprise AS 65000 will use eBGP to learn routes from ISP A and ISP B. Inside AS 65000, internal routers form iBGP sessions so they can forward traffic to the edge routers that learned those external routes. A frequent confusion is to assume that routes learned via iBGP are automatically redistributed by IGPs — iBGP only shares BGP attributes; you must ensure next‑hop reachability via your IGP and respect iBGP rules such as the split‑horizon behavior (iBGP speakers do not re-advertise routes learned from other iBGP peers by default). Remember: eBGP handles inter‑AS exchange, iBGP handles internal distribution of those external routes. Think about the enterprise with two ISPs: without iBGP, internal routers would not reliably learn how to reach external prefixes through the correct edge router.

BGP is classified as a path vector protocol because route advertisements carry the sequence of Autonomous Systems a prefix has passed through — the AS_PATH attribute. This explicit path information does two important things. First, it makes loop detection straightforward: if a router sees its own AS in the AS_PATH, it drops the route, preventing traffic from circulating indefinitely. Second, AS_PATH enables operators to make policy decisions based on which ASes are present or on path length. For example, if a route advertises AS_PATH [100 300 400], a router in AS 300 sees that the route passed through AS 100 and then came to 300; if 300 is the receiver and its own AS appears in the path, it will not accept that route due to loop detection. A practical enterprise example: when AS 65000 receives two routes to the same prefix, one with AS_PATH length 2 and another length 4, the operator might prefer the shorter AS_PATH as a simple tiebreaker or write policy that prefers routes avoiding specific ASes. A common misconception is to assume AS_PATH length always implies performance; AS_PATH conveys administrative traversal, not latency. Use AS_PATH for loop prevention and policy, but validate actual performance using telemetry and path testing.

Multi‑homing is when an enterprise connects to two or more ISPs simultaneously. BGP is the protocol that makes multi‑homing practical because it allows the enterprise to advertise prefixes to multiple upstream providers and to control which provider traffic uses for egress and ingress. In a typical setup, AS 65000 peers with ISP A (AS 100) and ISP B (AS 200) via eBGP. The enterprise advertises its public prefixes to both ISPs and learns external routes from both. To control outgoing traffic, the enterprise can set local preference or use AS_PATH prepending to make one path less attractive. For incoming traffic, BGP provides mechanisms to influence which ISP external networks prefer, though complete control is not guaranteed. The resilience benefit is straightforward: if one ISP link fails, BGP withdraws routes learned from that ISP and traffic naturally shifts to the remaining provider. A common novice error is to assume multi‑homing with BGP automatically yields equal load across ISPs; actual traffic distribution depends on global routing decisions and requires deliberate policy to shape. In practice, ensure your internal routers receive external routes via iBGP and that your IGP provides next‑hop reachability so failover occurs smoothly. Consider the enterprise example: test failover by simulating an ISP outage and observe route withdrawal and reconvergence to validate your policy and reachability behavior.

Now we'll walk through a simple labeling activity you will encounter in the assessment. Imagine Enterprise A — AS 65001 — and Enterprise B — AS 65002 — both connect to ISP AS 100. Each enterprise has two internal routers. The links between each enterprise and the ISP are eBGP peerings because they cross AS boundaries. Inside each enterprise, the internal routers form iBGP sessions so that routes learned from the ISP are available throughout the AS. To trace a prefix originating in AS 65001 and reaching a host in AS 65002, follow these steps: AS 65001’s border router advertises the prefix to AS 100 via eBGP; AS 100 propagates the route through its own AS and advertises to AS 65002 via eBGP; the border router in AS 65002 receives the prefix and uses iBGP to share it with its internal routers so the destination host can be reached. A frequent learner error is mislabeling internal pairings as eBGP or forgetting that the ISP‑to‑enterprise links are eBGP. As you label diagrams, confirm each peering's AS numbers: if they differ, it's eBGP; if they match, it's iBGP. Try drawing arrows for route advertisement direction to solidify your understanding.

In BGP terminology, a BGP speaker is simply a router running the BGP protocol that sends and receives route advertisements. A prefix is the network block being advertised, such as 192.0.2.0/24. When a BGP speaker advertises a prefix, it sends that prefix along with attributes like AS_PATH, next hop, and potentially MED or communities. The function of the BGP speaker is to originate, propagate, and apply policy to routes. For example, a border router in AS 65000 configured as a BGP speaker advertises its public prefix 198.51.100.0/24 to ISP peers. Those peers receive the prefix and add their own AS number to AS_PATH when they forward the route. A common misconception is to assume every router in the AS must be a BGP speaker; in many deployments a subset of edge and core routers speak BGP while others rely on internal distribution via iBGP and IGP. Another practical point is that prefixes must be announced intentionally: avoid accidentally advertising internal-only networks to the internet. In your design, choose which routers are BGP speakers, plan which prefixes to advertise, and ensure your policies prevent accidental leak of private addressing.

Remember the rule: different AS numbers mean eBGP; identical AS numbers mean iBGP. Second, neglecting IGP next‑hop reachability: BGP may advertise a route, but if your internal network cannot reach the route's next hop, traffic will blackhole. Third, assuming AS_PATH equals performance: AS_PATH records administrative traversal, not latency, so prefer measured metrics for performance-sensitive routing. Fourth, accidentally leaking prefixes: without careful export filters, you might advertise internal or private prefixes to the internet. Finally, not planning for multi‑homing behavior: traffic distribution is influenced by remote AS policies; don’t assume symmetric inbound/outbound flows. Each misconception can be mitigated by disciplined planning: verify AS numbers on diagrams, ensure IGP reachability, use route filtering to prevent leaks, and test failover scenarios to confirm behavior.
